title: perf-regression-alert-triage-dashboards-bisect
content:
Purpose:
This is a working notes / runbook for triaging performance regressions in the serving runtime. Focus areas: instrumentation sanity checks, dashboard panels to consult, quick bisect approaches (config vs commit), canary comparison methodology, and escalation steps for high-severity alerts.

Context and common scenarios:
- Alert fired: p99 API latency increased > 2x for a customer or route.
- Canary drift: a canary cluster shows higher token latency than baseline after a deploy.
- Cost regression: tokens/sec dropped leading to higher unit cost.
- Infra-level regression: GPU utilization lower but latency higher (possible stalls / memcpy issues).

High-level triage checklist (0-30m):
1) Confirm alert and scope
   - Which route/model/customers are affected? Check alert payload and Grafana tags.
   - Is the regression global, region-specific, or single-customer?
   - Check recent deploys (last 60m / 6h) in prod and canary.
2) Quick health signals
   - Query error rate and success rate for the route (last 30m).
   - Compare p50/p90/p99 latencies vs 24h and 7d baselines.
   - Check throughput (requests/s) and tokens/s to rule out workload shift.
3) Resource signals
   - GPU utilization, GPU memory, CPU steal, host load, network RX/TX.
   - CUDA memcpy/launch metrics if available; check stall counters.
4) Reproduce locally if possible
   - Run a small synthetic workload against the same model variant and input size used in the alert.

Instrumentation and dashboards to consult (ordered):
- Core API dashboard: p50/p90/p99 token latency, requests/s by route, error rates, request queue lengths (if present).
- Model performance dashboard: sequence-length distribution, KV cache hit rates, batch sizes, tokens/sec, generation time breakdown (compute vs memcpy vs queue).
- GPU node dashboard: per-GPU utilization, SM utilization, memory bandwidth, PCIe RX/TX, cudaMemcpy time, PCIe stalls, power limits.
- Canary vs baseline panel: side-by-side latency percentiles for canary and baseline (overlay with percent delta).
- Recent deploys panel: list of commits, PRs, config changes, and who deployed.
- Autoscaler / batching metrics: average batch size over time, batch formation latency, queue wait time.

Quick queries/examples to run (Prometheus / ClickHouse style pseudo-queries):
- p99 latency for route X over last 6h vs 24h baseline: "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=\"/v1/generate\", model=\"m1\"}[5m])) by (le))"
- Batch size distribution: "histogram_quantile(0.9, sum(rate(batch_size_bucket[5m])) by (le, model))"
- KV cache hit rate: "sum(rate(kv_cache_hits[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_lookups[5m]))"

Initial interpretation guide (rules of thumb):
- If p99 increases but tokens/sec also increased proportionally: likely workload shift (larger inputs or more concurrent requests).
- If p99 increases and GPU utilization decreased: look for stalls, memory thrashing, or serialization in host side (e.g., long memcpy, GC).
- If p99 increases and batch size decreased: batching regressions or config change affecting batching_timeout/limits.
- If canary shows regression but baseline does not: likely code/config change in the canary deploy.

Bisect strategies:
A) Config bisect (fast, common)
- Hypothesis: a config change (batching, quantization profile, kernel flag) caused regression.
- Steps: compare canary config to baseline; restore previous config flags incrementally to isolate culprit.
- Use quick toggles: disable batching optimization X, revert quantization fallback, turn off new kernel path.

B) Commit bisect (slower, accurate)
- Hypothesis: a code change in serving runtime introduced regression.
- Steps: use canary commit range (the deploy diff) and run binary search across commits.
- Limits: need test harness that reproduces the workload. Prefer using internal perf harness with synthetic traces rather than live traffic.
- Practical approach: run 2-3 representative commits first (old, mid, new) to see monotonicity, then binary search if needed.

Canary comparison checklist (when canary drift detected):
- Confirm canary and baseline use identical model versions and model artifacts (weights, quantization).
- Check hardware parity: same GPU type, driver, CUDA/cuDNN versions.
- Compare runtime flags: kernel selection, fused-kernel toggles, batching timeouts.
- Snapshot a few sample requests and run them side-by-side with profiling enabled to capture per-layer latencies.

Profiling tools and quick commands:
- Lightweight: enable per-request timing middleware (collect per-layer durations and emit to trace).
- NVTX + CUPTI traces for deep dives (requires capture and offline analysis).
- Perf counters: sample SM utilization and memory throughput during representative runs.
- CPU sampling: pprof-style sampling of host agent when memcpy or serialization suspected.
- If using remote profiler, remember to scrub customer data and use synthetic inputs where possible.

Escalation and communication model:
- Severity definitions:
   - Sev-1: >2x p99 increase and affecting >10% of traffic or key customers SLA breach.
   - Sev-2: noticeable degradation localized to region/canary or affecting internal SLAs.
- For Sev-1: paging SRE, on-call serving runtime lead, and product clearance. Create incident in Incident Tool and add link to this doc.
- For Sev-2: create a triage ticket in the perf-triage board and assign to eng-serving-runtime owner.
- Communication: Slack #serving-runtime-alerts + incident channel, update every 15m during active investigation.

Playbook: step-by-step when an alert fires
1) ACK alert and post findings (scope, initial health signals) in Slack.
2) Run the quick health signals checklist.
3) If canary shows regression -> compare configs and revert canary to last-known-good config.
4) If baseline and canary both degraded -> check infra and autoscaling; consider rolling back deploy.
5) If rollback not possible, add mitigation: increase capacity, increase batching timeout, or divert traffic to a healthy region/variant.
6) After mitigation, schedule deeper investigation (bisect or profiler capture).

Investigation notes / heuristics (common root causes we've seen):
- Regression introduced by kernel selection changes that accidentally hit a slower code path for specific sequence lengths.
- New quantization fallback that triggers non-optimized path for some layers.
- Batching timeout tweaks reducing average batch size dramatically under bursty traffic.
- Memory fragmentation causing slower allocations and more host-GPU memcpy.
- Driver upgrade that changed memcpy performance characteristics on some GPU instances.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Add a dashboard panel that shows percent of requests hitting new kernel path (feature flag label).
- Add synthetic canary workload with 3 traffic profiles (short, medium, long seq) that runs every 15m and stores results.
- Improve runbook automation: when p99 on canary > baseline by 30%, auto-compare config diffs and surface candidate flags.

References and related docs:
- perf-regression-triage-playbook (working doc)
- perf-regression-tracking-and-triage-notes (history and previous incidents)
- perf-regression-bisect-and-canary-notes (examples of past bisects)

Next steps (action items):
- [Marcus] Add the kernel-path percent panel to the canary dashboard (owner: Marcus) - due: 2026-02-20.
- [Aisha] Create a cron synthetic canary job for three profiles (short/med/long) - due: 2026-02-27.
- [Diego] Draft an automated config-diff comparator prototype for triage slack posts - due: 2026-03-06.

Notes-to-self / informal reminders:
- When running NVTX traces, capture both host and device timestamps to correlate memcpy spikes.
- Keep an incident log snippet in the triage ticket with the Prom queries used so we can reproduce quickly.
- If root cause is infra (driver/GPU) coordinate with infra and SRE to avoid repeated rollbacks.

(End of working notes)
